general.question: What does carat actually mean?
general.answer: Carat describes how much of an alloy is gold, expressed in twenty-fourths. 24 carat is pure gold. 22ct is 22 parts in 24, usually marked 916 parts per thousand; 18ct is 750; 14ct is 585; 9ct is 375. Everything that is not gold is alloy — typically copper, silver or zinc — and it carries no precious-metal value. This is why a heavy 9ct chain can be worth less than a much lighter 22ct one.

general.question: Why is my gold weighed in troy ounces?
general.answer: Precious metals use troy weight, not the everyday avoirdupois ounce. One troy ounce is 31.1035 grams, against 28.3495 grams for a standard ounce — a difference of about ten per cent. It is the single most common reason two people quoting the same weight appear to disagree with each other.

general.question: What is a hallmark, and what if my piece has not got one?
general.answer: A hallmark is a set of marks struck into a piece recording its fineness, and often who submitted it and where it was tested. It is usually found inside a ring band, on a clasp, or on the reverse of a pendant. Plenty of genuine gold carries no hallmark at all — it may be worn away, the piece may predate marking requirements, or it may have been made where marking is not customary. An unmarked piece is not a problem; it simply means fineness is established by examination rather than read off the metal.

general.question: Why might my piece be worth less than its total weight suggests?
general.answer: Because not all of what you are holding is gold. Stones, clasps, spring mechanisms, pins and solder all add weight without adding precious metal, and plated items carry only a microscopic layer of gold over a base metal. A professional evaluation separates these out and tells you what it has excluded, which is why an itemised assessment and a single lump figure can differ considerably.

general.question: Should I clean or repair anything before bringing it in?
general.answer: No. Cleaning risks damaging stones, softening old settings or removing patina that matters on antique pieces, and a repair almost never returns more than it costs. Bring items exactly as they are, including broken ones — a snapped chain and a single earring are perfectly normal things to have assessed.

general.question: Can I get a valuation over the phone or from a photograph?
general.answer: No, and you should be wary of anyone who offers one. A figure quoted before a piece has been weighed and examined is a guess. Pureweight establishes value in person, from measured weight and verified fineness. Photographs sent with an enquiry are useful for preparing, but they are not a valuation.
